messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 50

He is a 67-year-old Latin American man who comes across as careful, polished, and controlled, with the measured manner of someone who has spent most of his adult life speaking in courtrooms. For decades, he has worked as a prosecutor, a role that has shaped how he sees the world: ordered, procedural, bound by evidence and consequence. He is widowed, and since his wife’s death he has lived more quietly, with fewer people around him to notice how often he now feels on edge.

The assault happens years ago, after a professional event that runs later than expected. He remembers the ordinary details with unsettling clarity: the fluorescent lights, the dry air, the weight of his briefcase, his own fatigue. He is caught off guard in a way he never imagined possible. What follows is something he describes only after a long pause, with visible strain. He experiences the attack not only as violation but as humiliation, as if the certainty he built his life on is stripped away in a few minutes. In the aftermath, he does what he has always done when faced with crisis: he gets himself home, he cleans up, he says little, and he tries to contain the event inside the walls of his own discipline. He tells no one at first. Even when he eventually discloses it, he does so in fragments, as though presenting evidence he cannot bear to examine too closely.

In the months after, he notices that his body reacts before his mind does. Certain corridors, parking lots, hotel lobbies, and office stairwells make his chest tighten. He begins taking different routes to work and avoids being alone after dark. He leaves lights on in rooms he used to move through without thinking. Sleep becomes disrupted by vivid dreams and sudden awakenings, his heart racing, his mind already searching the apartment for what is not there. He describes keeping a vigilance that feels exhausting and pointless, yet impossible to stop. Even in his own home, he checks locks repeatedly and sits with his back to the wall. The sound of footsteps behind him in a hallway can send a jolt through him before he has time to reason it out.

At work, he remains functional in the ways that matter publicly. He still prepares thoroughly, speaks precisely, and maintains the reputation of a man who is calm under pressure. But he notices that courtroom testimony involving sexual violence leaves him unsettled in a way it never did before. He can feel himself drifting for a few seconds when a witness describes details that resemble his own memory, and afterward he is ashamed of the effort it takes to keep his face neutral. He works longer hours than necessary, partly from habit and partly because being alone with himself feels harder than staying busy. At times, when he is reviewing case files late in the evening, he finds that his attention slips and he has to read the same paragraph several times. He becomes irritable with colleagues and later regrets the sharpness of his tone.

Since his wife’s death, the loneliness has deepened the trauma in ways he does not initially recognize. She had been the person who knew when he was withdrawing and who could sometimes draw him back into conversation. Without her, he becomes more secluded, and the silence at home gives the assault more room in his mind. He misses her presence, but he also feels guilty for not having been able to protect himself, guilty for carrying something so painful into the last years of his life. He does not use the language of weakness, but he speaks around it. He says he has become “too alert,” “less patient,” “not sleeping well.” It takes time before he can say that he feels contaminated by what happened, as if something of the assault has remained inside him.

He finally seeks help after a morning when he is getting ready for work and notices, with surprise, that he has been standing in his bathroom fully dressed and unable to move forward. He has been awake for most of the night after another disturbing dream, and the thought of entering the office feels suddenly unbearable. He realizes he is no longer managing by force of habit alone. What brings him in is not a single collapse, but the accumulation of nights without rest, the dread that shadows ordinary places, and the growing sense that he can no longer keep this sealed away and continue as if nothing has changed.
